claims.text: The nanoscale platinum-group catalyst has high activity, selectivity, and durability for ethanol oxidation.
Its catalytic performance is governed by dynamic formation and optimal surface coverage of adsorbed intermediates.
Bridging CO, acetate, and acetaldehyde are key adsorbed intermediates on the catalyst.
These adsorbed intermediates modulate electron- and proton-transfer steps during ethanol oxidation.
The intermediate layer enables a balance between rapid complete ethanol oxidation and resistance to catalyst poisoning.
The catalyst can be represented as a nanoscale multimetallic or Pt-rich platinum-group alloy operating under direct-ethanol-fuel-cell conditions.
Complete ethanol oxidation proceeds through a 12-electron and 12-proton process.
An optimal adsorbed-intermediate layer facilitates efficient electron and proton transfer.
Avoidance of excessive adsorbed CO accumulation protects the catalyst from poisoning.
Changing applied potential or electrolyte composition predictably changes the surface coverage of the proposed intermediates.
Changes in intermediate coverage correlate with changes in catalytic current and product selectivity.
Operando spectra will exhibit distinct, potential-dependent changes in bands assigned to bridging CO, acetate, and acetaldehyde.
Under unlabeled-ethanol conditions, spectral features of the proposed intermediates will correlate with catalytic-current onset and magnitude.
Using carbon-13-labeled ethanol will shift the relevant vibrational bands and confirm that the detected intermediates derive from ethanol.
The proposed mechanism applies under typical direct-ethanol-fuel-cell operating conditions.
The proposed coverage-performance relationship may fail at extreme potentials, extreme pH, or in electrolytes containing strongly adsorbing alternative anions.
Overlapping spectral features and operando detection limits may distort the quantitative relationship between spectral intensity and catalytic current.
The relative contributions of the proposed intermediates may vary with catalyst composition and surface morphology.

contradictions.description: The uncertainty field acknowledges that detection limits and overlapping bands can prevent observation or quantification of intermediates, while the falsification rule treats absence of the expected spectral changes as disproof. Thus, the stated null result could arise from an admitted measurement limitation rather than failure of the mechanism.
